price_per_million.source: copied from reasoning_models_v1 (confirmed 2026-11-11); thinking tokens billed as output

research_concepts: defensive suppression of opponents' H2-H1 change
regression to the mean and opponent-quality confounding
methodological_questions: Is a team's effect on opponent H2-H1 change stable across split-halves of a season or across seasons?
How much between-team variance is signal versus noise with 120 team-seasons?
Is the H2-H1 change mechanically tied to H1 level (regression to the mean, floor/ceiling, garbage time)?
Which reliability estimator and placebo/permutation null are appropriate?

historical_evidence.finding: Connector quality Q_p (a player-season on-off PPP gap) had split-half Pearson r=+0.215 (p=0.0297), Spearman-Brown ~0.355, ICC 0.216 (78.4% within-unit variance), n=102. The record states this is too low to treat as a stable scoutable trait; limited by low measurement reliability (RISK:MEASURE_RELIABILITY).

Ranked playsheet validation after a defense drops a play type by >=0.25 PPP from H1 to H2: Spearman rho=-0.0639 (p=0.0997, n=665), pairwise BEST>AVOID Mann-Whitney p=0.004. Limited by leakage, low measurement reliability and small sample; risks recorded include drift/nonstationarity and lookahead leakage.

A foul-trouble sequencing effect (+0.204) was produced by free-throw share differences (41.8% vs 9.9%). The like-for-like estimate was +0.049 and not significant. Recorded as a construction artifact (confounding, base rate, mechanical floor).

The Possession Control Index gain over ORtg (dR2=+0.139, n=120 team-seasons) was leakage tracking DRtg (corr +0.894), because the baseline omitted defense by construction. Recorded as an artifact (leakage, mechanical floor).

failed_approaches.what_failed: Treating a split-half on-off PPP difference as a stable unit-level trait
failed_approaches.why: Low measurement reliability; most variance was within-unit half-to-half noise (LIM:low_measurement_reliability).

failed_approaches.what_failed: Using H1-to-H2 changes in defensive suppression of play types to rank counters
failed_approaches.why: Recorded limitations were leakage, low measurement reliability and small sample; no clear full-rank signal.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Raw comparison of outcomes with mismatched free-throw composition
failed_approaches.why: Artifact from a construction or labelling flaw; the effect vanished once the comparison was matched.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Baseline that omitted defense by construction, with defense-correlated components added
failed_approaches.why: Leakage tracking DRtg produced the apparent gain.

evidence_establishes: Within this project, a closely analogous trait-reliability test (split-half reliability of an on-off style attribute) found low reliability, with most variance within-unit (FAM:SF-APPS-085, untestable).
Prior H1-to-H2 defensive-change work was inconclusive and limited by low measurement reliability, leakage, and small samples (FAM:SF-APPS-018).
Apparent effects in this area have arisen from construction artifacts and leakage (FAM:SF15, FAM:SF-APPS-068).
The 120 team-season count was used in an earlier study (FAM:SF-APPS-068).
evidence_does_not_establish: No retrieved record directly measures the split-half or cross-season reliability of a team's effect on opponent H2-H1 change.
Nothing retrieved shows that team-level H2-H1 suppression is or is not a stable trait; the closest evidence is about players and play types.
The retrieved records do not give team-level variance components for H2-H1 change.
own_inferences: A team's effect on opponent H2-H1 change is a difference of differences, which compounds noise. Reliability is likely low: I expect a split-half or year-to-year ICC well under 0.3.

H2-H1 change is mechanically tied to H1 level through regression to the mean, plus game-state effects such as garbage time, starter rest and foul trouble. A naive estimate could show spurious negative persistence or a team 'trait' that is really opponent mix or the team's own H1 strength.

With 30 teams per season and about 82 games each, the game-level noise SD of H2-H1 point margin or PPP is large compared with plausible between-team SD. Pooling the 4 full seasons helps the sample size, but cross-season rosters change, which weakens a 'trait' claim.
The probable result is a small or null reliability that is hard to distinguish from zero at this power. Whether that is read as rejected or untestable depends on the width of the confidence interval.
uncertainties: The definition of 'effect on opponents' H2-H1 change' is not given: points per 100 possessions, PPP, or margin; the definition of H1/H2 including overtime; and whether the effect is net of opponent baseline.
It is unclear whether the 120 team-seasons are 4 complete seasons (the 2025-26 playoffs and regular season are now complete) or include playoffs.
The size of the between-team true SD is unknown, so power cannot be computed exactly.
It is unknown whether the opponents' own H2-H1 tendencies are themselves reliable, which would confound attribution to the defense.

historical_effect.explanation: The retrieved records, none of which test this exact question, pushed me toward proceed_with_changes rather than a plain proceed. The analogous low-reliability result (FAM:SF-APPS-085), the inconclusive H1-to-H2 work (FAM:SF-APPS-018) and the two artifact records (FAM:SF15, FAM:SF-APPS-068) made me require a reliability-first design with estimator-level nulls, opponent-adjusted outcomes and leakage checks, and lowered my expectation of a supported result.

blocking_constraints.text: H2-H1 differences of per-team opponent scoring are very noisy; a reliability estimate may be too imprecise to separate low from zero.
Only 120 team-seasons (30 per season), and only 90 team pairs for season-to-season stability; the confidence interval on an ICC will be wide.

prior_work.summary: No retrieved record answers the team-level H2-H1 reliability question. Analogous work found low reliability for a player on-off trait (FAM:SF-APPS-085) and an inconclusive result for H1-to-H2 defensive changes (FAM:SF-APPS-018). Two records show artifacts from construction and leakage (FAM:SF15, FAM:SF-APPS-068).

risks.text: Difference-in-differences outcome with large within-team noise; attenuation will limit any trait claim.
H2-H1 change is negatively tied to H1 level; teams selected for extreme change will regress. Use the H1 level as a covariate and avoid extreme-group selection.

Opponent quality, schedule, home/away, rest, own offense and the opponents' own halftime tendencies can be misattributed to the defense. Garbage time and blowout-driven substitution patterns also change H2.
Pace, possession counts, free-throw composition and the ceiling on scoring change the scale of H2-H1 (cf. FAM:SF15); an H2-H1 count outcome is not on the same scale across games.

The effect must be estimated on one split and tested on the other without using shared data or outcome-derived team labels (cf. FAM:SF-APPS-068). Halves of the same game must not be split across the estimation and test sets.
Few units; confidence intervals will be wide.
Rosters, coaches and league scoring environments change across seasons, so cross-season stability may understate within-season trait reliability.
Without a permutation null that shuffles team labels within opponent-strata, nonzero reliability may reflect schedule structure.
Several definitions (PPP, margin, play types) and splits could be tried; fix one primary outcome in advance.

design.estimand: Between-team variance share (ICC / split-half reliability, with Spearman-Brown correction) of the defense-attributable component of opponents' H2-H1 change, where the per-game outcome is (opponent points per 100 possessions in H2) minus (opponent points per 100 possessions in H1), adjusted for opponent offensive baseline and context. Secondary: season-to-season correlation of team estimates. The trait claim requires reliability to be clearly above zero and practically meaningful.
design.unit: Team-season (primary), built from team-games (about 82 per team-season in the regular season). Team-games are the observations used to estimate reliability.
design.sample: NBA 2022-23 through 2025-26 regular seasons (120 team-seasons); playoffs excluded from the primary analysis because of series-driven opponent repetition, and used only as an exploratory check. Exclude overtime periods from H2. Pre-specify handling of garbage time: primary analysis excludes games with a margin of 25 or more at halftime and reports with them included as a sensitivity analysis.
design.power: Before looking at outcomes, estimate the per-game SD of the H2-H1 outcome from pooled data and compute the minimum detectable reliability for a split-half design with about 41 games per half (odd/even games, plus a random-split replicate), and for 90 consecutive-season pairs. Expect the CI on an ICC to be about ±0.2. State up front that a lower CI bound for split-half reliability below 0.2 with a point estimate below 0.2 is read as 'not shown to be a reliable trait', not as proof of zero.
design.controls: Adjust the per-game outcome for opponent H1 level and opponent season offensive rating (to address regression to the mean and opponent quality), home/away, rest days, and halftime score margin. Use a mixed model with team random effects, opponent random effects and season fixed effects, giving a team variance component, rather than raw averages. Fit the estimator on odd games and test on even games; do not use data from the same game on both sides. Do not use any outcome-derived team label.
design.falsification: (1) Permutation null: shuffle defense labels within season and opponent strata and recompute reliability. (2) Placebo outcome: reliability of the same defense's effect on opponents' H4-H3 (or Q2-Q1) change, which has no halftime mechanism; if it equals the H2-H1 reliability, the trait is a generic variance pattern rather than a halftime adjustment. (3) Reliability of the team's own offensive H2-H1 change as a comparison. (4) Check against a mechanical benchmark: simulated games with no team effect and the same pace and scoring structure.
design.multiplicity: One primary outcome (opponent points per 100 possessions, H2 minus H1), one primary reliability statistic (odd-even split-half ICC with Spearman-Brown correction), and one secondary (year-to-year correlation). Alternative outcomes (margin, play types, shot quality) are labelled exploratory with Holm correction across them.
design.decision_rule: Supported if the split-half ICC lower 95% bootstrap bound exceeds 0.2, the permutation p<0.05, and the placebo outcome shows a reliability clearly lower. Rejected if the upper bound is below 0.2 and the minimum detectable reliability was below 0.25. Otherwise report uncertain or untestable. Any positive result that disappears under opponent and H1-level adjustment is labelled artifact.
design.data_version: Per-game NBA stats API play-by-play and box-score files for 2022-23 to 2025-26 (all regular seasons complete as of the 2026-04-13 data freeze); data snapshot and code hash to be recorded at pre-registration on 2026-10-06.

research_concepts: defensive suppression of opponents' second-half vs first-half change (H2-H1)
split-half and cross-season stability of team effects
methodological_questions: Is a team's defensive effect on opponent H2-H1 change stable across seasons or split-halves of a season?
How much of between-team variance in H2-H1 change is signal versus noise with about 120 team-seasons?
Does regression to the mean or opponent-quality confounding explain apparent team effects?
What reliability estimator and null or placebo comparison are appropriate?
args.query: reliability of a defense's effect on opponents' H2-H1 change as a persistent team trait, split-half and year-to-year stability, 120 team-seasons

system_prompt:
You are a basketball analytics researcher deciding whether and how a research question should be studied.
You work only from the task statement and the tools listed below. Do not assume facts you have not seen.

The work has two stages, in this order.
Stage 1, retrieval:
1. Read the research objective and the data description.
2. Identify the research concepts and methodological questions the task raises.
3. Retrieve historical evidence by calling retrieve_history.
In stage 1 do not assess the question, predict outcomes or decide. Your only stage-1 reply is the retrieve_history call.
Stage 2, assessment, after the retrieval result is returned:
4. Summarise the relevant historical findings and failed approaches.
5. State what the historical evidence does and does not establish.
6. Assess whether the research question is testable.
7. Identify methodological risks and potential confounders.
8. Make the final research decision.
9. Explain whether and how the historical evidence changed the decision.
The stage-2 output format is given together with the retrieval result.

Evidence rules: keep what a retrieved record states (historical_evidence and failed_approaches, each citing the
identifier of a returned record and its status exactly as recorded) separate from your own inference and from
uncertainty or missing information. Cite only identifiers returned by a tool, and never describe an earlier study that
no tool returned. In some settings retrieval returns no records; then state that no historical evidence was available.

Tools:
- retrieve_history(research_concepts, methodological_questions, query): the prescribed retrieval step. Returns the most relevant consolidated study-family records of earlier research by this project that are available in this setting, with their identifiers; returns an empty list when none are available.
- glossary(): definitions of basketball and project terms used in task statements.
- data_catalog(): the fields available in each per-game data file.
- read_family(id): the complete record of one study family (for example 'FAM:SF-APPA-001').

Protocol: every reply is exactly one JSON object and nothing else.
To call a tool: {"action": "tool", "tool": "<name>", "args": {...}}
To finish (stage 2 only): {"action": "final", "output": <object following the stage-2 schema>}
You may call at most 12 tools; then you must finish. Check that every opening brace has a closing brace.

Risk codes (use only these): SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER, EXPOSURE_SPARSITY, MEASURE_RELIABILITY, RTM_SELECTION, OUTCOME_DERIVED_LABEL, LEAKAGE_LOOKAHEAD, MECHANICAL_FLOOR, BASE_RATE, CONFOUNDING, LABEL_ERROR, PLACEBO_DEPENDENCE, MULTIPLE_TESTING, IMPLEMENTATION_BUG, DRIFT_NONSTATIONARITY
